title: How do we split a big number into its place values?
description: Farhan reads big distance numbers at a bus stand in Lucknow. The video splits each number into the value of every digit and shows why a zero adds no part.
teaching_notes: One idea: each non-zero digit gives one part worth its place value, and a zero gives none. Watch for a digit placed in the wrong column, such as the six of eight thousand and sixty two taken as hundreds.

source: Let Us Do (second set) 7, expanded form
video_script.why: The child can read a big number, but has not yet written it as a sum of the value of each digit.
video_script.substitution: Split each number by the value of its digits; a zero place is left out.
video_script.anchor: Farhan reading big distance numbers off the board at the Lucknow bus stand
video_script.wrong_answer: the six is worth six hundred
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu reads the six of eight thousand and sixty two as six hundred. The six sits in the tens place, so it is worth sixty.
video_script.payoff_line: each digit keeps its own place value

final_answer.spoken: eight thousand, sixty and two for the first number

maths_rules: a zero digit gives no part
slip: 8,062 split as 8,000 + 600 + 2 = 8,602, which is not 8,062
video_script.design: Exercise. Hint: each digit keeps its place value and a zero adds nothing. The number 783, done in the book, sits on the board; each split slides out under its digit.

beats.on_screen: a photo of the bus stand sits behind as a dimmed backdrop and fades at the end of the beat; a small title card From your book; a distance board at a bus stand shows 8,062, 9,980, 10,304, 23,004 and 70,405; a split arrow sits beside each number

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.board: a distance board appears with five big numbers
marks.ask: a split arrow appears beside each number

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='board'/>Farhan stands at the Lucknow bus stand and reads big numbers off the distance board.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Your book asks us to split five of them into the value of each digit.

beats.on_screen: the items hold still and the anchor gets an accent underline

marks.stop: the anchor is underlined in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Stop the video. Say your answer out loud.

beats.on_screen: the number 783 splits into 700, 80 and 3, each digit sliding under its place name; the words expanded form appear; a note says a zero has no value so leave it out

marks.parts: 700, 80 and 3 slide out under their digits
marks.name: the words expanded form appear

narration: <bookmark mark='done'/>Look at the number your book has done for you, seven hundred and eighty three.
<bookmark mark='parts'/>The seven is worth seven hundred, the eight is worth eighty, and the three is worth three.
<bookmark mark='name'/>Splitting a number into the value of each digit is called expanded form.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>A zero has no value, so leave its place out. Try again with this.

beats.on_screen: Chintu's bubble shows 8,062 = 8,000 + 600 + 2; the digit 6 is lit in the tens column; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.chintu: Chintu's bubble appears with the wrong split
marks.place: the six is lit in the tens column
marks.strike: the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='chintu'/>In eight thousand and sixty two, the six is worth six hundred.
<bookmark mark='place'/>Look at where the six sits. It is next to the ones place, so it is worth sixty.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>The hundreds place holds a zero, so it adds nothing.

beats.on_screen: the board shows 8,062 = 8,000 + 60 + 2 with the empty hundreds place greyed, then 9,980 = 9,000 + 900 + 80 with the empty ones place greyed

marks.b2: the empty hundreds place is greyed
marks.c2: the empty ones place is greyed

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Each digit keeps its own place value, so every digit that is not zero gets a part.
<bookmark mark='b'/>Eight thousand and sixty two splits into eight thousand, sixty and two.
<bookmark mark='b2'/>The hundreds place is zero, so no hundreds part is written.
<bookmark mark='c'/>Nine thousand nine hundred and eighty splits into nine thousand, nine hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='c2'/>The ones place is zero, so no ones part is written.

beats.on_screen: the board shows 10,304 = 10,000 + 300 + 4 with the tens place greyed, then 23,004 = 20,000 + 3,000 + 4 with the hundreds and tens places greyed

marks.d2: the empty tens place is greyed

narration: <bookmark mark='d'/>Ten thousand three hundred and four splits into ten thousand, three hundred and four.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>The tens place is zero, so it adds nothing.
<bookmark mark='e'/>Twenty three thousand and four splits into twenty thousand, three thousand and four.
<bookmark mark='e2'/>Here the hundreds and tens places are both zero.

beats.on_screen: the board shows 70,405 = 70,000 + 400 + 5 with the thousands and tens places greyed
narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Seventy thousand four hundred and five splits into seventy thousand, four hundred and five.
<bookmark mark='f2'/>The thousands place and the tens place are zero, so they add nothing.

beats.on_screen: the five splits sit in a column; an arrow adds the parts of 8,062 back to 8,062

marks.check: the parts of 8,062 add back to 8,062
marks.ask: the zero places glow once more

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>To check, add your parts back together and see if you get the number you started with.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Does your answer have one part for each digit that is not zero?
